title: Battle of Trafalgar
wiki_lead:
The Battle of Trafalgar was a fleet action fought on 21 October 1805 off Cape Trafalgar between the Royal Navy and a combined fleet of the French and Spanish navies during the Trafalgar campaign of the War of the Third Coalition. As part of Napoleon's planned invasion of the United Kingdom, the French and Spanish navies planned to take control of the English Channel and provide the French invasion army with safe passage to England. A Franco-Spanish fleet under French Vice-admiral Pierre-Charles Villeneuve sailed from Cádiz on 18 October 1805 and three days later encountered a British fleet under Vice-Admiral of the White Horatio Nelson, 1st Viscount Nelson in the Atlantic along southwestern Spain.
Nelson sailed his fleet directly at the Franco-Spanish line of battle's flank in two columns, hoping to break the line into pieces. Villeneuve foresaw Nelson's tactic but failed to prepare for it; the crews of the French and Spanish ships in contrast to their British counterparts were inexperienced, poorly trained and suffered from low morale. Nelson's plan worked brilliantly with both columns splitting the Franco-Spanish fleet in three groups, isolating the rear. The Franco-Spanish vanguard sailed ahead while attempting to turn back, leaving the British temporarily superior in number against the remainder of Villeneuve's fleet. 18 French and Spanish ships were ultimately captured or destroyed while the British lost none.
Nelson's approach exposed the leading ships of the British columns to intense crossfire as they approached the Franco-Spanish lines. Nelson's own HMS Victory led the front column and was almost knocked out of action. Nelson was shot by French marksman during the battle and died shortly before it ended. Villeneuve was captured along with his flagship and later attended Nelson's state funeral while a captive on parole in Britain. Following the battle, the senior surviving Spanish commander, Lieutenant-general Federico Gravina, led part of the surviving Franco-Spanish fleet away from the storm; he died six months later of wounds sustained during the battle.
Nelson's victory against the odds and death during battle secured his place as a British national hero. His signal to the fleet shortly before the battle, "England expects that every man will do his duty", is regularly quoted and paraphrased. The victory confirmed Britain's naval supremacy in the Napoleonic Wars and was achieved in part through Nelson's departure from prevailing sailing ship tactics. The battle led to the definitive end of any real efforts by Napoleon to invade Britain, and although it had a limited impact on the War of the Third Coalition resulted in Britain's command of the sea not being tested for over a century.

grok_lead: The Battle of Trafalgar was a pivotal naval engagement during the Napoleonic Wars, fought on 21 October 1805 off the southwest coast of Spain near Cape Trafalgar, in which a British fleet of 27 ships of the line, commanded by Admiral Horatio Nelson aboard HMS Victory, decisively defeated a combined French and Spanish fleet of 33 ships under Vice Admiral Pierre-Charles Villeneuve. The battle lasted approximately five hours and resulted in the capture or destruction of 18 to 20 enemy vessels, with no British ships lost, though Nelson was mortally wounded by a French sniper and died aboard his flagship later that day. This victory thwarted Napoleon Bonaparte's plans for an invasion of Britain and established unchallenged British naval dominance on the seas for over a century. The conflict arose from Napoleon's strategy to neutralize the Royal Navy and enable a cross-Channel invasion, prompting Villeneuve to combine forces with the Spanish fleet at CÃ¡diz after earlier maneuvers in the West Indies. Nelson, who had pursued the enemy fleet across the Atlantic, blockaded CÃ¡diz for weeks before engaging when the Franco-Spanish ships sailed out on 19 October. Employing his innovative " Nelson Touch " tactic, Nelson divided his fleet into two columns to break the enemy line astern, allowing superior British gunnery to concentrate fire at close range rather than adhering to the conventional parallel-line formation. The battle commenced around noon with the lead British ship, HMS Royal Sovereign under Vice Admiral Cuthbert Collingwood, drawing initial fire, followed by intense close-quarters combat that left the allied fleet in disarray. Casualties were starkly asymmetrical, reflecting British tactical superiority: approximately 449 British sailors were killed and 1,217 wounded, compared to over 4,400 killed and 2,545 wounded on the French and Spanish side, with around 20,000 allied personnel taken prisoner. A severe storm the following day sank many of the captured prizes, but the outcome remained a resounding triumph for Britain. Historically, Trafalgar not only ended the immediate threat of invasion but also boosted British morale and naval prestige, contributing to Napoleon's eventual downfall by isolating his continental campaigns from overseas support. Nelson's death, marked by his famous signal "England expects that every man will do his duty," transformed him into a national icon, symbolizing sacrificial leadership in defense of the realm.
